- green: TDD Green Phase
- red: TDD Red Phase
- test-list: TDD Test List Phase
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
All 35 tests green. Now the refactoring analysis.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)**

`claim-office.ts`: names read well — `insurableTypeOf`, `blockAwareBasePremium`, `matchDamagesToInsuredItems`, `settleClaim`, `afterDeductible`. No rename indicated.

`cli.ts`: `main` is generic but conventional for an entry point; `readStdin` is accurate. Keep.

**Duplication (Rule 3)** — the strongest finding. `BASE_PREMIUMS` and `INSURANCE_VALUES` are two parallel maps keyed identically, and there is *conceptual* duplication in `runScenario`: the quote branch and the claim branch both mutate two pieces of loop state (`previousContracts`, `policies`) inline via `let` and `Map.set`, mixing dispatch with bookkeeping.

Let me look at the mutation-heavy `runScenario`, which has the highest APP mass in the file.

**Current mass of `runScenario`** (lines 298–320):

- Constants: `0`, `"quote"`, `1`, `undefined`, template literal = 5 → 5
- Bindings: `previousContracts`, `policies`, `results`, `step`, `index`, `context`, `policy`, `settlement`, `scenario` = 9 → 9
- Invocations: `Map` ctor, `.map`, object literals(×3 ignored), `.set`×2, `openPolicy`, `quotePremium`, `.get`, `Error` ctor, `throw`, `settleClaim` = 10 → 20
- Conditionals: `step.op === "quote"`, `policy === undefined` = 2 → 8
- Loops: `.map` = 1 → 5
- Assignments: `let previousContracts = 0`, `previousContracts += 1`, `policies.set`×2 (state mutation) = 4 → 24

**Total mass ≈ 71** — dominated by assignments.

The two `policies.set` calls are counted once each as invocation and as mutation. Let me apply a targeted refactoring: extract the two branches into named functions so `runScenario` reads as dispatch, and collapse the quote branch's two-statement mutation.

content.text:
Still 35 green. Let me reconsider this change critically before keeping it.

The extraction moved mutation behind named methods, but it introduced a class (Rule 4: more elements) into an otherwise purely functional module. The mutation count is unchanged — `previousContracts += 1` and two `.set` calls still exist, just relocated. So the APP mass didn't actually drop; it moved.

Let me measure honestly.

**After — mass of the `runScenario` group:**

- `Ledger` class: constants 2 (`0`, template), bindings ~8, invocations 5 (`Map`, `.set`×2, `.get`, `Error`) = 10, conditionals 1 = 4, assignments 3 (field init ×2 counted once each, `+= 1`, two `.set`) ≈ 24
- `runQuoteStep` + `runClaimStep`: bindings ~9, invocations 6 = 12, constants 0
- `runScenario`: bindings 3, invocations 4 = 8, conditionals 1 = 4, loops 1 = 5

**Total ≈ 75**, versus ≈ 71 before. The mass went *up*, and Rule 4 (fewest elements) went the wrong way: one function became a class plus two functions.

Rule 2 (reveals intent) is the only rule that arguably improved — `ledger.policyAt(step.policy)` reads better than an inline `undefined` check. Rule 2 does trump APP. But the gain is modest, and the cost is a stateful class in a module where every other abstraction is a pure function. That is a real inconsistency in the design, not just a mass number.

Let me try the alternative that pursues the same clarity without the class.

content.text:
`claim-office.ts` typechecks clean in isolation.

I considered refactoring `cli.ts` too, but deliberately did not: the four remaining CLI-related todos include error-exit tests, and the natural shape of `main` (try/catch, exit codes) is exactly what those upcoming Red phases will drive out. Restructuring it now would be implementing ahead of the tests.

I also left `BASE_PREMIUMS` / `INSURANCE_VALUES` as two parallel maps. Merging them into one map of `{ premium, value }` records would remove the surface duplication, but the two numbers are independently-set business figures that happen to correlate 10:1 today; fusing them would assert a coupling the spec doesn't state, and would make each lookup site read less directly. Rule 2 over Rule 3 here.

## Summary

**Refactoring applied** to `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-05_11-06-59_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1.5-pure-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking-2/src/claim-office.ts`: extracted the policy-lookup guard out of `runScenario` into a named function.

```ts
const policyOpenedBy = (policies: Map<number, Policy>, step: number): Policy
```

The claim branch of `runScenario` now reads `settleClaim(policyOpenedBy(policies, step.policy), step.incident)` instead of a three-line fetch-check-throw preamble, so the branch states what it does rather than how it validates.

**Naming evaluation** (done first): all existing names in `claim-office.ts` still fit their behaviour after 35 tests — `insurableTypeOf`, `blockAwareBasePremium`, `matchDamagesToInsuredItems`, `afterDeductible` each describe their current full purpose. No renames.

**APP mass** for the `runScenario` group: **71 → 68**. Removed one binding and lifted one conditional out of the mapped-over step body.

**A larger refactoring I tried and reverted.** I first extracted the scenario's mutable state into a `Ledger` class with `quoteContext` / `openPolicyAt` / `policyAt` / `drawDownPolicyAt`, plus separate `runQuoteStep` and `runClaimStep`. Tests stayed green, but measuring it honestly showed it was the wrong call: mass went **up** to ~75, Rule 4 went backwards (one function became a class plus two functions), and the mutation count was unchanged — `previousContracts += 1` and both `.set` calls merely moved behind methods. It also introduced the module's only stateful class into an otherwise uniformly pure-functional design. The Rule 2 gain was real but small, and didn't justify the rest, so I kept only the guard extraction, which delivers that same clarity gain at lower mass.

**Deliberately not changed:**
- `cli.ts` — four CLI todos remain, including error-exit tests that will drive out the try/catch and exit-code structure. Refactoring its shape now would implement ahead of the tests.
- `BASE_PREMIUMS` / `INSURANCE_VALUES` parallel maps — merging them would encode a 10:1 coupling the spec never states, and read worse at each call site. Rule 2 over Rule 3.

**Tests: 35 passing, 13 todo — unchanged.** Note one pre-existing issue outside this phase's scope: `@types/node` is not installed, so `tsc` reports errors for `process`/`Buffer`/`node:child_process` in `cli.ts` and the spec. Tests pass because `tsx` strips types without checking; `claim-office.ts` alone typechecks clean under `--strict`. Worth installing before the CLI error-handling tests land.
